This page reads three corpora with `quanteda`: archived tweets from the November 2021 Biden–Xi summit, presidential documents I collected from the *Compilation of Presidential Documents* (CPD) on GovInfo, and the inaugural addresses since 1945. It also has YouTube comments on the October 2025 Trump–Xi meeting in Busan. Answers are labeled with the question numbers from the assignment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.textstats)
library(quanteda.textplots)
library(quanteda.textmodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(rvest)
library(knitr)

cpd_dir <- "data/cpd"
htm_dir <- file.path(cpd_dir, "htm")   # listed in .gitignore
yt_dir  <- "data/youtube"
tw_dir  <- "data/summit"               # listed in .gitignore
walk(c(htm_dir, yt_dir, tw_dir), dir.create, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# save each API response once, then read the saved copy
cached <- function(path, f) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) saveRDS(f(), path)
  readRDS(path)
}

now_central <- function() format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z", tz = "America/Chicago")
pct <- \(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
num <- \(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
theme_set(theme_bw())

# keyness plot with room for the longest labels
plot_keyness <- function(key, n = 20) textplot_keyness(key, n = n, labelsize = 3.5, margin = 0.2)
```
:::

My copy of `quanteda_textanalytics01.R` from Teams covers Part 1: the summit tweets, LSA, the hashtag and mention networks, and sentiment with `sentimentr` and `syuzhet`. It has no code for Parts 2 and 3, so I wrote those from the assignment and the [quanteda tutorials](https://tutorials.quanteda.io): basic operations and `kwic()` (ch. 3), frequency, lexical diversity, keyness and similarity (ch. 4), and Wordfish (ch. 6, "Scaling and classification"). The GovInfo key from Assignment 5 and a YouTube Data API key are in `~/.Renviron` and are read with `Sys.getenv()`. Both are sent in request headers, so they are not on this page, in the logs or in the repository.

## 2a. One summit, two kinds of text

### 2a.i. The public: summit tweets


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summit <- cached(file.path(tw_dir, "summit.rds"), \(x) {
  read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/datamethods/master/textanalytics/summit_11162021.csv",
           show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(status_id, created_at, text, is_retweet, lang)
}) |>
  mutate(text = str_replace_all(text, "&", "&"))

low <- str_to_lower(summit$text)
tw <- list(n = nrow(summit), first = min(summit$created_at), last = max(summit$created_at),
           retweets = mean(summit$is_retweet), english = mean(summit$lang == "en"),
           xi = mean(str_detect(low, "\\bxi\\b")), biden = mean(str_detect(low, "biden")),
           old_friend = sum(str_detect(low, "old friend")), guardrails = sum(str_detect(low, "guardrail")),
           rules = sum(str_detect(low, "rules of the road")))

sum_twt <- summit$text
```
:::


The dataset has 14,520 tweets from November  7 to November 16, 2021 (UTC). 62% are retweets and 93% are in English. The file does not record the search query, but 88% of the tweets contain "Biden" and 85% contain "Xi". It was collected with the Twitter API, which no longer offers this access, so it cannot be collected again.

**Frequent words.** Stopwords, URLs, hashtags and mentions are removed here; they get their own networks below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tw_words <- tokens(sum_twt, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_url = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE) |>
  tokens_remove(c(stopwords("en"), "amp", "rt", "#*", "@*")) |>
  dfm()

textstat_frequency(tw_words, n = 25) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(feature, frequency), y = frequency)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Frequency", title = "Most frequent words in the summit tweets")
```

The hashtags link the summit to other topics: `#coronavirus` and `#fentanyl` in the main cluster, a separate cluster on `#uyghurs`, `#tibetans` and `#humanrights`, and `#taiwan`. The most mentioned accounts are `@potus` and `@joebiden`, then news accounts and reporters. In the network, the accounts that appear together form small clusters: reporters around `@politico`, and `@eneskanter` with NBA accounts. Those last tweets are about Uyghur and Tibetan activists at a Wizards game and the NBA player Enes Kanter, urging Biden to raise human rights with Xi at the summit.

**LSA.** The script keeps four dimensions (`nd = 4`). I ran it on the cleaned word matrix, keeping words that appear in at least 5 tweets. These are the words with the largest loadings on each dimension:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lsa_dfm <- dfm_trim(tw_words, min_docfreq = 5)
sum_lsa <- textmodel_lsa(lsa_dfm, nd = 4)

as_tibble(sum_lsa$features, rownames = "feature") |>
  pivot_longer(-feature, names_to = "dimension", values_to = "loading") |>
  group_by(dimension) |>
  slice_max(abs(loading), n = 10) |>
  summarise(top_words = paste(feature, collapse = ", ")) |>
  kable()
```

### 2a.ii. The government: Compilation of Presidential Documents

The CPD is the official record of the President's public remarks, statements and orders, compiled by the Office of the Federal Register (OFR). I searched the CPD collection through the GovInfo API, paged through every result, took each package's summary for metadata, and downloaded each document's text from `/packages/{packageId}/htm`. The functions are the ones from Assignment 5. `govtdata01.R` only downloads from an exported list, so in Assignment 5 I wrote the API search and download with `httr2`. Here I reuse them and log each file.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# every GovInfo call goes through this; the key comes from .Renviron and goes in a header
govinfo <- function(path) {
  request("https://api.govinfo.gov") |>
    req_url_path_append(path) |>
    req_headers(`X-Api-Key` = Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY"), .redact = "X-Api-Key") |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3)
}

cpd_query <- 'collection:(CPD) AND "Xi Jinping" AND publishdate:range(2021-01-20,)'

search_page <- function(query, offset_mark = "*") {
  govinfo("search") |>
    req_body_json(list(query = query, pageSize = 100, offsetMark = offset_mark,
                       sorts = list(list(field = "publishdate", sortOrder = "DESC")))) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json()
}

search_all <- function(query) {
  out  <- list()
  mark <- "*"
  repeat {
    page <- search_page(query, mark)
    if (length(page$results) == 0) break
    out  <- c(out, page$results)
    mark <- page$offsetMark
    if (is.null(mark)) break
  }
  bind_rows(map(out, \(r) r[c("packageId", "title", "dateIssued", "lastModified")]))
}

cpd_found <- cached(file.path(cpd_dir, "cpd_search.rds"), \(x) {
  list(searched = now_central(), results = search_all(cpd_query))
})
ids <- unique(cpd_found$results$packageId)
c(results = nrow(cpd_found$results), distinct = length(ids))
```

A CPD document is not all the President's words. Transcripts label each turn ("The President.", "Q." for a reporter, "Secretary Rubio.", "President Xi."). The OFR editors add subject headings inside transcripts ("China-U.S. Trade"), bracketed notes ("[Laughter]"), and at the end a note, categories, and an index of the names mentioned. So I split each document into the president's words, other speakers, and the editors' text. The speaker labels are found with a regular expression. It is a heuristic: a few paragraphs that start with a name, like a list of companies, are taken as another speaker.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# transcripts label each turn ("The President.", "Q.", "Secretary Rubio."); a paragraph
# without a label continues the last speaker, and an unlabeled document is all the president's
president_re <- "^(The President|President Biden|President Trump)\\. "
reporter_re  <- "^Q\\. "
word_re      <- "(?:(?:Mr|Mrs|Ms|Dr|Lt|Col|Capt|Maj|Gen|Sen|Rep|Gov|Comd|U\\.S)\\.|[A-Z][A-Za-z'’-]*|of|de|da|la|bin)"
other_re     <- paste0("^(?!(?:And|But|So|Alright|Okay|Well|Yes|No|Now|Oh|On|Go|Happy|That.s|Thank|Thanks|Good|Great|Right)\\b)",
                       "(?:", word_re, " ){1,5}[A-Z][A-Za-z'’-]+\\. ")

label_turns <- function(paras) {
  # a few paragraphs hold more than one turn
  paras <- unlist(str_split(paras, "\\s(?=(?:Q|The President|President Biden|President Trump)\\. )"))
  # the editors add subject headings ("China-U.S. Trade") and bracketed notes ("[Laughter]")
  heading <- nchar(paras) < 120 & !str_detect(paras, "[.?!:;,—–\"”’)…\\]]$")
  bracket <- str_extract_all(paras, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]") |> map_chr(\(x) paste(x, collapse = " "))
  text    <- str_squish(str_remove_all(paras, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]"))
  speaker <- case_when(heading ~ "heading",
                       str_detect(text, president_re) ~ "president",
                       str_detect(text, reporter_re)  ~ "reporter",
                       str_detect(text, other_re)     ~ "other",
                       .default = NA_character_)
  last <- "president"
  for (i in seq_along(speaker)) {
    if (is.na(speaker[i])) speaker[i] <- last
    if (speaker[i] != "heading") last <- speaker[i]
  }
  tibble(speaker, text = if_else(heading, paras, str_remove(text, president_re)), bracket)
}

# split each document into the president's words, other speakers, and what the OFR editors added
split_cpd <- function(file) {
  paras <- read_html(file) |> html_elements("p, h1") |> html_text2() |> str_squish()
  paras <- paras[paras != ""]
  end   <- detect_index(paras, \(p) str_detect(p, "^(\\[Filed|NOTE:|Categories:|Names:|Subjects:|DCPD Number:)"))
  if (end == 0) end <- length(paras) + 1
  # administration line, title, and the date line when there is one
  n_head <- if (str_detect(paras[3], paste0("^(", paste(month.name, collapse = "|"), ") \\d"))) 3 else 2
  turns  <- label_turns(paras[seq_len(end - 1)][-seq_len(n_head)])
  join   <- \(x) paste(x[x != ""], collapse = "\n")
  tibble(header          = paste(head(paras, n_head), collapse = " | "),
         president_words = join(turns$text[turns$speaker == "president"]),
         others          = join(turns$text[turns$speaker %in% c("reporter", "other")]),
         editors         = join(c(turns$text[turns$speaker == "heading"], turns$bracket,
                                  paras[seq_along(paras) >= end])))
}

meta <- imap(summaries, \(s, id) tibble(
  packageId  = id,
  dateIssued = s$dateIssued,
  title      = s$title,
  president  = s$president$id %||% NA_character_,
  category   = s$dcpdCategory[[1]]$level1 %||% NA_character_,
  pages      = as.integer(s$pages %||% NA)
)) |> list_rbind()

docs <- meta |>
  bind_cols(map(meta$packageId, \(id) split_cpd(file.path(htm_dir, paste0(id, ".htm")))) |> list_rbind()) |>
  mutate(admin        = if_else(president == "JRB", "Biden", "Trump"),
         xi_president = str_detect(president_words, "\\bXi\\b"),
         xi_others    = str_detect(others, "\\bXi\\b"),
         xi_editors   = str_detect(editors, "\\bXi\\b"),
         digest       = str_detect(packageId, "DIGEST|CHECKLIST"),
         xi_where     = case_when(digest ~ "annual digest or checklist",
                                  xi_president ~ "the president",
                                  xi_others ~ "only another speaker",
                                  xi_editors ~ "only the editors",
                                  .default = "nowhere in the text"))

use <- docs |> filter(!digest)
```
:::

In 12 documents Xi is named only by the editors, in the index of names or the note at the end (for example, "The memorandum referred to President Xi Jinping of China"). In 41 more, only a reporter or another leader says his name. The search matches the editors' index as well as the text, so it finds documents where the President never mentions Xi.

**Xi in context.** `kwic()` on the president's words, with a window of 7 words. Here are a few lines from each administration:

```{.r .cell-code}
cpd_corp <- corpus(use, text_field = "president_words", docid_field = "packageId")
cpd_toks <- tokens(cpd_corp, remove_punct = TRUE)
kw <- kwic(cpd_toks, pattern = "Xi", case_insensitive = FALSE, window = 7)

set.seed(6302)
kw |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(select(use, docname = packageId, admin, dateIssued), by = "docname") |>
  group_by(admin) |>
  slice_sample(n = 6) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(admin, dateIssued, pre, keyword, post) |>
  kable()
```

### 2a.iv. Optional: YouTube comments on the Busan meeting

I searched YouTube for "Trump Xi Busan", for videos published from October 29 to November 2, 2025, ordered by relevance, with English as the preferred language. Then I collected the top-level comments from every result that had comments. Replies are not included.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
yt <- function(endpoint, ...) {
  request("https://www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3") |>
    req_url_path_append(endpoint) |>
    req_url_query(...) |>
    req_headers(`X-goog-api-key` = Sys.getenv("YOUTUBE_API_KEY"), .redact = "X-goog-api-key") |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3)
}

yt_query <- list(q = "Trump Xi Busan", type = "video", order = "relevance", maxResults = 50,
                 publishedAfter = "2025-10-29T00:00:00Z", publishedBefore = "2025-11-03T00:00:00Z",
                 relevanceLanguage = "en")

yt_search <- cached(file.path(yt_dir, "search.rds"), \(x) {
  list(searched = now_central(),
       response = exec(yt, "search", part = "snippet", !!!yt_query) |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json())
})
video_ids <- map_chr(yt_search$response$items, \(x) x$id$videoId)

videos <- cached(file.path(yt_dir, "videos.rds"), \(x) {
  yt("videos", part = "snippet,statistics,contentDetails", id = paste(video_ids, collapse = ",")) |>
    req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
})
video_df <- map(videos$items, \(v) tibble(
  rank      = match(v$id, video_ids),
  videoId   = v$id,
  channel   = v$snippet$channelTitle,
  published = v$snippet$publishedAt,
  title     = v$snippet$title,
  duration  = v$contentDetails$duration,
  views     = as.integer(v$statistics$viewCount %||% NA),
  comment_count = as.integer(v$statistics$commentCount %||% NA)
)) |> list_rbind() |> arrange(rank)

get_comments <- function(id) {
  out   <- list()
  token <- NULL
  pages <- 0
  repeat {
    resp <- yt("commentThreads", part = "snippet", videoId = id, maxResults = 100,
               textFormat = "plainText", pageToken = token) |>
      req_error(is_error = \(r) FALSE) |>
      req_perform()
    if (resp_status(resp) != 200) break
    body  <- resp_body_json(resp)
    pages <- pages + 1
    out   <- c(out, body$items)
    token <- body$nextPageToken
    if (is.null(token)) break
    Sys.sleep(0.5)
  }
  list(status = resp_status(resp), pages = pages,
       comments = map(out, \(x) {
         s <- x$snippet$topLevelComment$snippet
         tibble(videoId = id, commentId = x$id, published = s$publishedAt,
                likes = s$likeCount, replies = x$snippet$totalReplyCount, text = s$textDisplay)
       }) |> list_rbind())
}

yt_log_file <- file.path(yt_dir, "collection_log.csv")
comments <- cached(file.path(yt_dir, "comments.rds"), \(x) {
  with_comments <- video_df |> filter(comment_count > 0)
  got <- map(with_comments$videoId, \(id) {
    res <- get_comments(id)
    Sys.sleep(1)
    res$log <- tibble(videoId = id, status = res$status, pages = res$pages,
                      comments_collected = nrow(res$comments), finished = now_central())
    res
  })
  map(got, "log") |> list_rbind() |> write_csv(yt_log_file)
  map(got, "comments") |> list_rbind()
})
yt_log <- read_csv(yt_log_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

video_manifest <- video_df |> left_join(select(yt_log, videoId, status, comments_collected), by = "videoId")
write_csv(video_manifest, file.path(yt_dir, "video_manifest.csv"))

video_manifest |>

  arrange(desc(comments_collected)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  transmute(channel, title = str_trunc(title, 60), views = num(views), comments_collected) |>
  kable()
```

## 4. Report

**Two kinds of text (2a.iii).** The tweets show what people on Twitter passed around during the summit week, and most of it was the news. 62% are retweets, and many repeat quotes from the opening remarks in the CPD transcript: "old friend" (1,197 tweets), "guardrails" (304), "rules of the road" (277). The hashtags and mentions add what the official text leaves out: COVID, fentanyl, Taiwan, and activists urging Biden to raise the Uyghurs and Tibet. The tweets cannot say what was agreed, and they are not a sample of the public. They were written by accounts that used the collector's keywords in that window, for their followers.

The CPD has the President's public words as spoken. For the summit it has one document, the remarks before the closed talks. Over five years it shows how each White House talked about China. Biden says "Xi Jinping" and retells his personal history with him. Trump says "President Xi" and talks about a great relationship, deals and tariffs. The White House produced these texts for the press and the public record, and the OFR edited them. They show how the presidents presented policy in public. They do not show how it was made. The 2025 YouTube comments were written by viewers of a few news videos, for other viewers, and are more about Trump than about China.

**Data-generating processes.** The tweets were chosen by a keyword and a collection window. So the frequent words and LSA describe what spread among those accounts, mostly retweets of a few posts. The CPD documents were chosen first by the White House (what it released), then by an OFR editor (what goes in, plus headings, notes and an index of names), and then by my query. The query matches that index, so 12 documents are in the corpus only because an editor listed Xi. The keyness compares what each White House released, including Trump's long press exchanges (787,645 words in 160 documents against 488,544 in 175). So it compares two ways of talking in public. It says little about the two China policies. The inaugurals were chosen by tradition: one speech per term, the same occasion, written for the nation. The 21 speeches are all there is, so differences between them come from the year and the speaker. With only 21, party keyness is weak.

**What Wordfish measures (3b).** Wordfish (Slapin and Proksch 2008) assumes each word count in a speech is drawn from a Poisson distribution, with a rate set by the speech's length, the word's overall frequency, and the speech's position on one hidden dimension times the word's weight on it. Words are independent of each other and their order is ignored. On the inaugurals the dimension seems to measure time. It correlates 0.87 with the year, and party adds nothing. Postwar words ("peoples", "resources", "program", "equality") are at one end; "thank", "everyone", "borders", "jobs" and "protect" are at the other. It could be the policy words of each era, or a change from formal to direct speech. To show what it measures I would need outside evidence: correlation with an independent measure (such as hand-coded tone or expert ideology scores), stable results when I change the preprocessing, and the same dimension found within one era. I must set `dir` because the model is identified only up to its sign. Flipping every position and word weight fits the data equally well. `dir = c(Truman 1949, Trump 2025)` puts Truman below Trump, so later speeches are on the positive side. Without it, the direction is arbitrary.

## Data note: the CPD collection


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
manifest <- docs |>
  left_join(select(dl_log, packageId, url, status, bytes, md5), by = "packageId") |>
  transmute(packageId, dateIssued, administration = admin, category, title, pages,
            included = !digest, xi_named_by = xi_where, url, status, bytes, md5)
write_csv(manifest, file.path(cpd_dir, "manifest.csv"))
```
:::


- **Source.** *Compilation of Presidential Documents* (collection CPD), published by the Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration, on GovInfo. Accessed through the GovInfo API (`api.govinfo.gov`): `/search`, `/packages/{id}/summary` and `/packages/{id}/htm`.
- **Permission.** Works of the US government are in the public domain (17 U.S.C. § 105). The API needs a free api.data.gov key. I waited 1 to 2 seconds between downloads, well under the rate limit.
- **Query.** collection:(CPD) AND "Xi Jinping" AND publishdate:range(2021-01-20,), sorted by publish date, paged 100 at a time, run on 2026-10-19 07:50:57 CDT.
- **Selection.** The search returned 344 packages, all downloaded (HTTP 200). I excluded the 9 annual digests and checklists, leaving 335 documents: 175 from Biden and 160 from Trump. The administration comes from each package's `president` field. Text analysis uses only the president's words, split from other speakers and from editors' headings, brackets and notes with the regular expressions above.
- **Gaps.** The search matches the editors' index of names, so 12 documents are included only because the editors list Xi, and in 41 more only a reporter or another leader says his name. A document where the President says only "Xi" and the editors do not list the full name could be missed. There are no results between January 20 and March 17, 2021, although Biden called Xi on February 10, 2021. That call appears only as a line in the 2021 Digest, not as a document of its own. The latest document is from 2026-09-12, so the CPD seems to run a few weeks behind, and there is no 2025 Digest yet. Translated remarks by foreign leaders and reporters' questions are in the documents but not in my analysis. The speaker split is a heuristic.
